steps.title: Your Italian Heritage
steps.subtitle: These four answers determine your eligibility, the route you'll take, and which documents you need.

questions.label: Which Italian-born ancestor connects you?
questions.hint: Decree-Law 36/2025 (in force 2025-03-28) limits new applications to descendants of an Italian-born parent or grandparent.

questions.label: When did your Italian ancestor emigrate from Italy?
questions.hint: Pre-1912 emigration affects whether naturalization broke the chain; post-1948 simplifies the maternal-line analysis.

questions.label: Did your Italian ancestor naturalize as a US citizen?

options.label: Yes — but AFTER the next generation in the line was born
Yes — BEFORE the next generation was born

questions.hint: If naturalization happened before the next generation in the line was born, the citizenship chain is broken.

questions.label: Does your line pass through a female ancestor whose child was born BEFORE January 1, 1948?
questions.hint: If yes, you must file in the Court of Rome (a '1948 case') rather than at a consulate.

steps.title: Your Plan & Timeline
steps.subtitle: Jure Sanguinis is a multi-year process. We'll back-date due dates from your target.

questions.label: When do you want to hold Italian citizenship?
Have you already booked a Prenot@Mi consulate appointment?

taskRules.description: DL 36/2025 (in force 2025-03-28) limits new applications to descendants of an Italian-born parent or grandparent. Great-grandparent paths filed after that date are largely closed except through court action.

taskRules.taskTitle: Consult a lawyer about great-grandparent eligibility post-DL 36/2025
taskRules.description: Your line runs through a great-grandparent (or further). Under the 2025 reform, consulate applications are no longer accepted. A specialist lawyer can advise whether court action or a different path remains open in your case.

taskRules.taskTitle: Verify the citizenship chain was not broken by naturalization
taskRules.description: If your Italian-born ancestor naturalized as a US citizen BEFORE the next generation in the line was born, the chain is broken. Before investing in documents, confirm naturalization timing via USCIS Genealogy.

taskRules.taskTitle: Plan your '1948 case' in the Court of Rome
taskRules.description: Because your line passes through a female ancestor with a child born before 1948-01-01, consulates will reject the administrative application. The court route is filed in Rome, decided in 18–36 months, and has a very high approval rate when the documentary chain is clean.

taskRules.taskTitle: Identify the Italian consulate with jurisdiction over your US residence
taskRules.description: Consulates only accept applications from residents within their jurisdiction. You cannot shop for shorter wait times. Find your consulate based on your state of residence.

taskRules.taskTitle: Order your Italian ancestor's birth certificate (atto di nascita)
taskRules.description: Contact the Comune (town hall) of birth in Italy directly, or via an agent. Request a multilingual extract (estratto plurilingue, Vienna Convention) which does not need translation. Allow 2–6 months.

taskRules.taskTitle: Order your Italian ancestor's marriage certificate (atto di matrimonio)
taskRules.description: From the Comune where the marriage took place. Same multilingual extract format as the birth certificate.

From USCIS Genealogy. If your ancestor naturalized, you need to prove the date was AFTER the next generation's birth. If they never naturalized, request a Certificate of Non-Existence of Record as proof.

taskRules.taskTitle: Order vital records for every generation in the chain (long-form)
taskRules.description: Birth, marriage, and death certificates for each generation between you and the Italian-born ancestor. Long-form (not short-form) — the consulate rejects abstracts.

taskRules.taskTitle: Apostille every US document in the chain
taskRules.description: Each state's Secretary of State office issues apostilles for state-issued records. Federal records (naturalization, FBI) are apostilled by the US Department of State. $5–$25 per document plus 2–8 weeks per submission.

taskRules.taskTitle: Get sworn Italian translations (traduttore giurato) of every US document
taskRules.description: Translations must be by a translator the Italian consulate recognizes, or sworn in Italy. Each consulate publishes its accepted-translator list online.

taskRules.taskTitle: Correct any name or date discrepancies in your documents
taskRules.description: If your great-grandfather appears as Giuseppe on his Italian birth record and Joseph on his US naturalization, you will need a court 'rettifica' or amended US records before submission. This is the most common cause of rejection — review every document line by line.

Italian consulates use the Prenot@Mi system. Citizenship appointments typically have 1–3 year waitlists — book as soon as documents are ordered, not when they arrive. If your consulate's queue is closed, monitor daily.

taskRules.taskTitle: Engage an Italian lawyer for your 1948 case
taskRules.description: Filed at the Court of Rome. Fees typically €3,500–€7,000 for the whole family. Pick a lawyer with a track record of 1948 cases and ask for referrals from prior US clients.

taskRules.taskTitle: Attend your consulate appointment and submit the dossier
taskRules.description: Bring originals and photocopies of every document. The ~€300 fee is paid at the appointment (form of payment varies by consulate). The consulate forwards your dossier to the relevant Italian Comune for registration.

taskRules.taskTitle: File your 1948 case in the Court of Rome
taskRules.description: Your lawyer files the petition with all apostilled + translated documents. You usually do not need to travel to Italy for the hearing.

taskRules.taskTitle: Wait for the Italian Comune to register your birth (trascrizione)
taskRules.description: After consulate approval (or court ruling), your records go to the relevant Comune for trascrizione. This typically takes 6–18 months. Once registered, you are an Italian citizen.

taskRules.taskTitle: Receive your codice fiscale and Italian passport
taskRules.description: Once registered with your Comune, the consulate issues your codice fiscale (Italian tax ID) and you can apply for an Italian passport — a full EU passport granting freedom of movement, residence, and work across the EU.

Anagrafe degli Italiani Residenti all'Estero — the required registry for Italian citizens living abroad. Registration is done through your consulate and is needed to vote and access consular services.

The US taxes citizens on worldwide income regardless of residence. Italy taxes residents (183-day rule). The US-Italy tax treaty covers most overlap. If you intend to retire in southern Italy, also research the 7% flat-tax regime.

taskRules.taskTitle: Register any children's births with the consulate
taskRules.description: Children born to you after you become Italian are automatically Italian, but the birth must be registered (trascrizione) with the consulate to take effect in Italy and the EU.
